headline: Three lawsuits now stand between Trump and his arch.
summary: DC and Virginia sued Saturday to block the 250-foot arch Trump wants at the bridge to Arlington National Cemetery. It would top the Statue of Liberty by 100 feet. Their filing says three years of building would snarl traffic and slow ambulances. That makes three suits. The government says work could start next week.

cover_question.q: Can a judge stop Trump's arch?

cover_answer: Pause it, yes. One judge said she'd decide fast.
table_question: Should the neighbors get a vote on what you build in your yard?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The president wants a giant stone arch near Washington, taller than the Statue of Liberty. The city next door and the state across the river asked a judge to stop it. They say three years of building would jam the roads, like a traffic cone that never moves. A judge decides, and nothing changes for you.
5-7.why: A statue-sized thing and a traffic jam: two pictures they already own. They can't follow a lawsuit yet, so the cone does that work. A six-year-old takes one vivid picture for the whole event, so the cone has to be the right one.
5-7.why_long: A child this age takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script hands them two they already own: taller than the Statue of Liberty, and a traffic cone that never moves. Who sued whom never comes up. Expect "will they build it?" Say a judge decides, and nobody knows yet.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Trump wants a 250-foot arch at the bridge to Arlington cemetery. Work could start next week. DC and Virginia sued Saturday: three years of building would jam the road and slow ambulances. They want a judge to pause it first, like a referee stopping play to check the call.
8-12.why: Plan, start date, objection, pause. This age wants to know who enforces a rule, and the referee is the enforcer they know.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules and who enforces them, so the script runs the chain: a plan, two governments that object, a judge who can pause it. The referee is the enforcer they know. Expect "can a judge really stop the president?" She can pause the work while the case is heard, and she said she'd be quick.

13-17.script: Who gets a say when the federal government builds on federal land in your city? DC and Virginia say nobody asked them, and sued. The White House says the arch honors veterans. Second: the judge asked what the rush was beyond "bedazzling the city." Is hurry a reason to stop someone?
13-17.why: Veterans and traffic are both true. They can hold both now, and will tell you which one carries.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the arch is meant to honor veterans, and two governments say it would jam their roads and nobody asked them. The script asks who gets a say, which is the legal question. Expect "so is the judge against Trump?" She asked a pointed question. Say whether a judge may.

5-7.q: Why don't they want the big arch?
5-7.a: They say building it would jam the roads for three years and slow down ambulances. A judge will decide.

8-12.q: Can a judge stop Trump's arch?
8-12.a: A judge can pause it while the case is heard. One said she'd be quick.
DC and Virginia are suing the Park Service, which would build it.

13-17.q: Who gets a say on federal land in a city?
13-17.a: DC and Virginia say nobody consulted them. A judge sorts it out.

13-17.q: Does "bedazzle the city" count as a reason?
13-17.a: The judge's word for the rush. The government's answer: "high priority."
